abstract: The Budget Lab at Yale's AI Labor Market Tracker, updated September 15, 2026 with August 2026 Current Population Survey microdata, again finds no clear evidence of AI-driven labor market disruption. The tracker (launched as an interactive July 16, 2026, replacing the earlier prose updates) has three parts: occupational churn (a dissimilarity index of the occupational mix, updated monthly), AI exposure and usage metrics (shares of workers by exposure group, AI task exposure among the unemployed, Anthropic usage-based automation/augmentation measures, updated monthly), and a synthetic differences-in-differences (SDID) comparison of AI-exposed and comparable unexposed occupations (updated quarterly). The current update says churn across occupations, AI exposure among the unemployed, and usage data all remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-AI trends. In the published data, the share of workers in the highest OpenAI-exposure group (top quintile, Eloundou et al.) was 18.16% in November 2022 and 18.24% in August 2026 (three-month moving average); the lowest group moved from 29.07% to 29.58% and the middle group from 45.82% to 45.06%. The SDID employment-share estimate for 2026Q2 is essentially zero (-0.000002, 95% CI -0.0078 to 0.0078 in the tracker's share units), and no post-2022 quarter is statistically distinguishable from zero. The Budget Lab stresses these findings may change as new data arrive.
keyFindings: 0 measurable AI-attributable US employment effect through August 2026 CPS: churn, exposure among the unemployed, and usage metrics are flat, within historical ranges, or on pre-AI trends
18.24% of workers were in the highest OpenAI-exposure group in August 2026, vs 18.16% in November 2022 (three-month moving average, top quintile by construction)

SDID employment-share gap between AI-exposed and synthetic unexposed occupations for 2026Q2: about 0 (-0.000002; 95% CI about +/-0.0078 in the tracker's share units); no quarter since 2022 is significant
SDID comparison now extends through 2026Q2; churn and exposure metrics are monthly through August 2026
The Budget Lab calls the takeaways provisional: 'these findings may change as new data become available'
methodology: Monthly CPS microdata (IPUMS-CPS), August 2026 release. Occupational dissimilarity index on a 12-month moving average vs recent and historical baselines; exposure metrics from Felten-Raj-Seamans, Eloundou et al., Eisfeldt et al., Tomlinson et al.; usage metrics from Anthropic Economic Index (Massenkoff et al. 2026); SDID of AI-exposed vs synthetic unexposed occupations for employment share, real hourly wages and unemployment (Clarke et al. 2022 inference), quarterly through 2026Q2. Figures in keyFindings come from the tracker's 'Download All Data' CSVs (ai-metrics/workers-by-exposure-level, comparisons/employment-shares).
qualifiers: Tier 1: institutional research venue with consistent public methodology and data; matches the tier of prior Budget Lab CPS updates. Caveats: a null finding means no detectable effect, not proof of zero effect; CPS occupational detail is coarse and the SDID confidence bands are wide relative to plausible early effects; exposure-group shares are fixed quintiles, so their stability shows no shift in the exposure mix of employment, not a level of exposure; usage data rely on Anthropic conversation mappings. The tracker does not claim AI will have no effect, only that it is not yet visible.
